lessons.title: Edward's Death and the Succession Crisis of 1066

before.content_html:
A Kingdom Without an Heir

On 5 January 1066, King Edward the Confessor died in his new abbey church at Westminster. He had reigned for 23 years but had no children. England in 1066 was rich, well-organised and dangerously unstable: it ran a sophisticated system of geld tax, struck high-quality silver coin, and supported around two million people. That wealth made the throne worth fighting for. By the spring of 1066 four men were preparing to take it.

Why the Succession Was Disputed

Anglo-Saxon England had no fixed law of succession. The throne usually passed to a close male relative, but the council of leading nobles — the Witan — had to confirm the choice. A king could also promise the throne to someone in his lifetime. Edward had made several different gestures over his long reign, and each of them now mattered.

On his deathbed, witnesses said Edward stretched out his hand to his most powerful earl, Harold Godwinson, and commended his queen and kingdom to him. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle accepted this as the decisive act. Norman writers, however, claimed Edward had already promised the crown to Duke William of Normandy back in 1051, and that Harold had sworn an oath to support William’s claim while a guest in Normandy in around 1064. The oath, real or invented, became the moral spine of the Norman case.

Key Fact

Four claimants pursued the English throne in 1066: Harold Godwinson (deathbed gesture and Witan election), William of Normandy (1051 promise and Harold’s oath), Harald Hardrada of Norway (a treaty inherited from King Cnut’s line) and Edgar Atheling (royal Anglo-Saxon blood).

Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex

Harold was the most powerful man in England outside the king. As Earl of Wessex he controlled the richest part of the kingdom; his brothers Tostig, Gyrth and Leofwine held Northumbria, East Anglia and Kent. The Godwins were also tied to royalty — Edward had married Harold’s sister Edith. Harold had led English armies, kept the Welsh border under control and was popular with the southern thegns. The Witan met on 6 January, the day of Edward’s funeral, and elected him king. He was crowned the same day at Westminster Abbey.

By Anglo-Saxon rules Harold’s position was strong. He had been chosen by the Witan, named by the dying king, and crowned in front of the leading nobles. The ‘usurper’ label comes from Norman writers like William of Poitiers, who needed to justify the invasion. Modern historians stress that until October 1066 most contemporaries inside England saw Harold’s rule as legitimate — the misconception that he was an obvious oath-breaker is post-conquest propaganda.

William, Duke of Normandy

William had ruled Normandy since 1035, fighting off rivals as a teenager and pacifying the duchy with castles and loyal lords. He claimed Edward had promised him the English throne during a visit in 1051, when Edward’s relations with the Godwin family had broken down. William also claimed that Harold, shipwrecked on the Norman coast in around 1064, had sworn a sacred oath to back William’s claim — an oath the Bayeux Tapestry shows being sworn over holy relics. To break such an oath was, by 11th-century standards, a serious sin, and William used this to win Pope Alexander II’s blessing for his invasion. A papal banner was sent to Normandy in 1066.

Harald Hardrada of Norway

Harald Hardrada (‘the Hard Ruler’) was the most feared warrior in northern Europe. He claimed England through an old treaty between his predecessor Magnus and Harthacnut, the Anglo-Danish king who had ruled before Edward. The claim was thin in law but Hardrada had ships, men and a record of victories from Sicily to the Black Sea. He was joined in summer 1066 by Tostig Godwinson, Harold’s exiled brother, who had been driven out of his Northumbrian earldom in 1065 and wanted revenge.

Edgar Atheling, the Forgotten Heir

Edgar was the last male of the old West Saxon royal line — grandson of Edmund Ironside, great-nephew of Edward the Confessor. By blood his claim was the strongest of all. But Edgar was about 14 in January 1066, with no military following and no powerful earl behind him. The Witan needed an adult king who could fight, not a teenage prince. Edgar would matter later, after Hastings, when he was briefly proposed as king before submitting to William.

By 1066 England had been raising the geld for over 60 years. Royal mints in around 70 towns produced standard silver pennies. Sheriffs collected fines and rents in every shire. The king’s personal landholdings (the royal demesne) made him the largest landowner in the country. For an outsider like William or Hardrada, capturing the English crown meant capturing one of the wealthiest, most centralised states in western Europe — far richer than Normandy.

Key Fact

The Witan elected Harold on 6 January 1066 because England needed an adult, battle-tested king. Edgar Atheling had royal blood but was too young; Harold had armies, allies and Edward’s deathbed gesture. By Norman standards he was an oath-breaker; by Anglo-Saxon standards he was the legitimate king.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘8 marks — Narrative Account’ on the events of 1066, examiners reward causal links rather than dates in a row. Don’t just say ‘Edward died, then Harold was crowned, then William prepared to invade.’ Show why each step caused the next: Edward’s deathbed gesture made Harold’s coronation possible; the coronation made William’s 1051 promise look like a broken oath; Hardrada’s decision to invade was triggered by Tostig’s exile and Harold’s vulnerability. Use connective phrases like ‘this meant that’, ‘as a result’ and ‘the consequence was’.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the succession crisis in England in 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Four rival claimants pursued the throne after Edward’s death — Harold Godwinson, William of Normandy, Harald Hardrada of Norway and Edgar Atheling — with overlapping claims based on promise, oath, treaty and royal blood.
• Edward the Confessor was childless, so the Witan had to choose a successor; this council of leading earls and bishops elected Harold on 6 January 1066.
• Edward’s deathbed gesture to Harold and an earlier 1051 promise to William created competing ‘promises’ that each side used to justify its claim.
• Harold had reportedly sworn an oath to support William while in Normandy around 1064, which Norman writers used to portray his coronation as oath-breaking.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail.]

practice_questions.text: Write a narrative account of the events that led to Harold Godwinson’s coronation as king in January 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Edward the Confessor’s long childless reign meant the question of succession was open well before his death; he had made gestures to William in 1051 and to Harold by 1066.
• On his deathbed Edward extended his hand to Harold and commended his kingdom to him; this gave Harold a public claim that the Witan could endorse.
• The Witan met immediately at Westminster on 6 January 1066, the day of Edward’s funeral, and elected Harold king because England needed an adult ruler to face the threats forming abroad.
• Harold was crowned the same day at Westminster Abbey, the first king to be consecrated in Edward’s new church — tying his rule symbolically to the dead king’s legacy.
• The result of these linked steps was that within 24 hours of Edward’s death, England had a new, anointed king — setting up the confrontations with William and Hardrada that would define the rest of the year.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal links between events.
Secure: Clear sequence with some causal links.
Developing: Sequence of events with limited links.
Emerging: Simple chronology; causal links missing.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of the Witan’s decision to choose Harold Godwinson as king in January 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Witan’s decision gave Harold immediate legitimacy under Anglo-Saxon custom — he was the formally chosen king of a unified, anointed realm.
• The choice meant Edgar Atheling, the only male of the old West Saxon line, was passed over — demonstrating that the Witan prioritised an adult, militarily capable ruler over royal blood.
• In the longer term it gave Norman writers their central propaganda point: from October 1066 onwards William’s side described Harold as an oath-breaker, an interpretation we now know was post-conquest framing.
• It shows the Anglo-Saxon system of elective kingship in action one final time before the Normans replaced it with hereditary, primogeniture-leaning succession.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of William of Normandy’s claim to the English throne.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William claimed that Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne during a visit in 1051, when relations between Edward and the Godwin family had collapsed.
• Norman sources insisted Harold Godwinson had sworn a sacred oath to support William’s claim while a guest in Normandy in around 1064, an oath taken over holy relics.
• William secured Pope Alexander II’s blessing in 1066, including the gift of a papal banner, which framed the invasion as righteous Christian reform.
• William was already a battle-tested ruler in Normandy, with a reputation for ruthless effectiveness that strengthened the credibility of his claim abroad.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edgar Atheling for the succession crisis of 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edgar represented the strongest blood claim to the throne — grandson of Edmund Ironside and direct male heir of the West Saxon royal line.
• His age (around 14) and lack of military following meant the Witan passed him over for Harold; this shows that Anglo-Saxon kingship in 1066 valued capability above pure descent.
• Significance over time: Edgar was briefly elected king after Hastings in October 1066 before submitting to William at Berkhamsted, which made him a rallying point for later revolts.
• The fact that the Witan chose an adult earl over a royal teenager helps disprove the Norman framing of Harold as an obvious usurper — the choice reflected the political reality of facing two foreign invasions.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from the year 1066, that personal ambition — rather than law or custom — was the most important factor in driving the succession crisis.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• Each claimant pressed his case because the prize was uniquely valuable: England’s geld revenue, mints and royal demesne made the throne worth fighting for.
• William chose to invade despite the risks of a sea crossing because his political position in Normandy depended on big victories abroad.
• Harald Hardrada’s claim through the old Cnut-Magnus treaty was thin; he pursued it because he was the most ambitious warrior in northern Europe and Tostig Godwinson’s exile gave him a pretext.
• Tostig’s personal grievance against his brother Harold turned a Norse expedition into a serious northern threat that forced Harold to fight at Stamford Bridge.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Anglo-Saxon custom — the role of the Witan, the importance of a deathbed gesture, the king’s right to nominate — framed every claim and made the Witan’s choice of Harold immediately legitimate inside England.
• Religious law gave William’s side decisive weight: the papal banner from Alexander II turned the invasion into a sanctioned crusade, which custom and ambition alone could not have produced.
• Edgar Atheling’s blood claim, rooted in inheritance custom, would resurface in revolts after 1066, showing that custom continued to matter.

A strong response weighs personal ambition against custom and law and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Stamford Bridge and Hastings: the Battles of 1066

before.description: Two battles in three weeks — Stamford Bridge and Hastings — and why Norman victory was.
before.content_html:
A Year of Two Invasions

By September 1066 Harold Godwinson had been king for eight months. He had spent the summer with the largest army England could field on the south coast, watching for William’s ships. Provisions ran out on 8 September and the army went home. Within a fortnight the wind he had been waiting for blew the wrong way: Harald Hardrada, not William, was the first to land.

Fulford Gate, 20 September 1066

Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson sailed up the Humber with around 300 ships and 9,000 men. The northern earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria gathered the local fyrd and met them at Fulford Gate, just south of York, on 20 September. The Norse line outlasted the English; Edwin and Morcar’s army was broken and York opened its gates. Hardrada now controlled the north.

The March North

Harold heard the news in London around 21 September. He summoned his housecarls, called out the southern fyrd, and rode north. He covered roughly 185 miles in four to five days — an exceptional pace for an 11th-century army. He arrived at Tadcaster on 24 September, picking up local levies as he came.

Stamford Bridge, 25 September 1066

Hardrada had agreed to meet hostages from York at Stamford Bridge, seven miles east of the city. His men had left their mail behind in the ships at Riccall, expecting nothing more than ceremony. Harold’s fast march caught them by surprise. After heavy fighting, including a famous stand by a single Norse warrior on the bridge itself, the English broke through. Hardrada was killed by an arrow to the throat; Tostig was killed in the melee. Of around 300 ships only 24 returned to Norway. Stamford Bridge was a comprehensive English victory — and the last great battle of the Viking Age in Britain.

Key Fact

At Stamford Bridge on 25 September 1066, Harold’s housecarls and southern fyrd destroyed Harald Hardrada’s Norse army. Hardrada and Tostig Godwinson were both killed. Only 24 of about 300 Norse ships sailed home.

William’s Landing on the South Coast

Three days later, on 28 September, William’s fleet landed unopposed on the Sussex coast at Pevensey. He moved his base to Hastings within days and threw up a wooden castle there. His men ravaged the local countryside, partly for supplies, partly to force Harold to march and fight before his army could fully recover. Harold marched south with his housecarls and the surviving fyrd, gathering reinforcements as he went, but his army was tired and depleted before the battle began.

Hastings, 14 October 1066

Harold reached the area on 13 October and chose his ground well. He drew up his men on Senlac ridge, blocking the Hastings–London road. The English formed a tight shield wall on the crest of the ridge: housecarls in the front rank with two-handed Dane axes, fyrd behind them. William attacked uphill with three lines — archers, infantry, then mounted knights.

Norman archers shot first but their arrows had little effect against the shield wall on higher ground. The infantry charge was thrown back. The cavalry charge stalled. A rumour ran through William’s left flank that the duke had been killed; it began to break. William rode bare-headed along the line to show he was alive, rallied his men and charged again. Sometime in the afternoon a section of the English right pursued retreating Bretons down the slope — whether by genuine retreat or feigned retreat is debated — and were cut down by the cavalry on the open ground. The shield wall thinned. Late in the day Harold was killed; the Bayeux Tapestry shows him struck in the eye, then cut down by a mounted knight. With the king dead and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine already fallen, the housecarls fought to the death around the standard. The fyrd dispersed into the woods.

Why Hastings Was Close-Run

It is tempting to assume Norman cavalry and archers always beat an Anglo-Saxon shield wall, but the battle was decided in the last hour of daylight. The English had repulsed two major Norman attacks. Harold’s army was depleted from Stamford Bridge and the rapid march, but the ridge negated William’s cavalry advantage for most of the day. Modern historians stress the role of the feigned (or genuine) retreats and the death of Harold himself: had Harold survived to night, William’s army — far from supplies, in hostile country, with no reinforcements — might have had to retreat to its ships. The myth of inevitable Norman victory grew up after the conquest, written by the winners.

Norman armies fought with three arms working together: archers softened the enemy line, infantry advanced under cover of the shooting, and mailed knights on warhorses charged on command. They also brought prefabricated castles — Hastings was fortified within days of landing. The Anglo-Saxons fought on foot in massed shield walls, with elite housecarls swinging two-handed Dane axes capable of cutting through mail. Both ways of war could win; the question was who controlled the ground.

Key Fact

Hastings was decided in the last hour of daylight on 14 October 1066. The shield wall had repulsed Norman archers, infantry and the first cavalry charge. The combination of feigned retreats, the wearing-down of the housecarls and Harold’s death — not Norman tactical superiority alone — turned the battle.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Effects’ question on Hastings, the highest band rewards effects that link directly to wider depth-study themes — conquest, control, the change of ruling class — not just ‘the English lost the battle’. Pick two consequences and develop each: e.g. Harold’s death meant no remaining adult male of Godwin or Wessex line, opening the way to William’s coronation; the destruction of the housecarls eliminated England’s elite professional soldiers, leaving no force capable of resisting William in the field for years afterwards.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Battle of Stamford Bridge.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was fought on 25 September 1066, seven miles east of York, between Harold Godwinson’s English army and Harald Hardrada’s Norse force supported by Tostig Godwinson.
• Harold surprised the Norse by marching about 185 miles in four to five days from London, catching Hardrada’s men without their mail at the bridge.
• Both Harald Hardrada and Tostig were killed, and only about 24 of the original 300 Norse ships returned to Norway.
• A famous Norse warrior held the bridge against the English advance until he was speared from beneath through the timbers.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Harold’s victory at Stamford Bridge on the Battle of Hastings three weeks later.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Stamford Bridge wore down Harold’s elite housecarls and southern fyrd, so the army that fought at Hastings was depleted in numbers and physically tired.
• Casualties at Stamford Bridge meant Harold could not call on the same numbers of trained warriors at Hastings — the shield wall had fewer men in its rear ranks.
• The need to march back south at speed (250+ miles) prevented Harold from waiting for further reinforcements from the Midlands and the North, particularly Edwin and Morcar.
• On the other hand, the Stamford Bridge victory removed the second front entirely — without it, Harold would have faced two invasions simultaneously, which would almost certainly have destroyed his rule before October.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and clear causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Anglo-Saxon shield wall at Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Housecarls formed the front rank, equipped with mail, helmets and two-handed Dane axes capable of cutting through Norman mail.
• The fyrd, the general levy of able-bodied freemen, stood in the ranks behind, supplying numbers and replacing fallen housecarls.
• Shields were locked edge-to-edge in a continuous wall, with spears braced over the top, on the crest of Senlac ridge to negate Norman cavalry advantage.
• The formation held repeated archer volleys, infantry assaults and the first major cavalry charge; it was only thinned by feigned retreats and Norman repeat attacks late in the day.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Battle of Hastings on the political situation in England in late 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Harold and his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine were killed, eliminating the entire Godwinson leadership and removing the only adult military rivals to William inside England.
• The destruction of the housecarls meant no professional army was left to fight William in the field; later resistance in 1067–71 had to rely on revolts and sieges, not pitched battle.
• Edgar Atheling was briefly proposed as king by the Witan but had no troops to back him; with the southern earls dead and Edwin and Morcar still recovering from Fulford, no plausible alternative could be assembled in time.
• William’s subsequent march via Dover, Canterbury and Berkhamsted forced submissions one after another, leading to his coronation at Westminster on 25 December 1066.

Mastering: Multiple effects with named events and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of military innovations — cavalry, archers and combined arms — for the outcome of the Battle of Hastings.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the combination of archers, infantry and mailed knights gave William flexibility on the day — when one arm failed, he could feed in another and resume the assault.
• Archers were significant in that they kept pressure on the shield wall throughout the day; later traditions claimed an arrow finally struck Harold, though contemporary sources are unclear.
• Cavalry on its own did not win the battle — the first major charge stalled against the ridge; significance lay in cavalry working with feigned retreats to peel off sections of the English line.
• Significance over time: combined arms and the prefabricated castle at Hastings became templates for William’s next 20 years of conquest, marking a permanent shift in how war was waged in England.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from the campaigns of 1066, that William’s victory at Hastings was the result of luck and circumstance rather than tactical superiority.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The wind turned in William’s favour just as Harold’s southern army had stood down on 8 September after running out of provisions, so William landed unopposed at Pevensey.
• Harold was forced to fight Stamford Bridge first; without that distraction his army would have been fresh and full strength at Hastings.
• The shield wall held until late afternoon; Harold’s death — whether from an arrow, a knight, or both — was the accident that broke a battle that had otherwise gone to the English.
• William’s personal escape from a panic on the left flank, riding bare-headed to rally his men, depended on luck as much as leadership.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Combined-arms tactics — archers, infantry and cavalry working together — were a genuine Norman tactical innovation that the English shield wall was not designed to face.
• Feigned retreats, even if some were genuine, required disciplined cavalry able to regroup under fire — a real tactical achievement.
• William’s decision to fortify Hastings within days of landing showed strategic foresight; he could fall back on the castle if defeated.
• Pope Alexander II’s blessing and the papal banner gave the Norman army a moral and recruiting advantage that was political planning, not luck.

A strong response weighs luck and circumstance against tactical and strategic decisions, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the campaigns with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: From Hastings to Coronation: William Takes the Throne

before.description: How William turned a battlefield win into a crown — submissions, castles and the Christmas.
before.content_html:
From Battlefield to Throne

A battlefield victory was not a country. After Hastings on 14 October 1066, William held only the field and the camp. London, Winchester, York and the Welsh borders were untouched. The remaining English leaders — Edwin and Morcar in the Midlands and North, the surviving thegns, the bishops, the Witan — could still raise an army or proclaim another king. The next ten weeks decided whether Hastings would be remembered as the start of a conquest or a one-off raid.

The March of Submissions

William moved cautiously. He waited five days at Hastings for an English surrender that did not come. He then turned east along the coast, taking Romney and Dover. Dover’s castle was strengthened in eight days. From there he pushed inland to Canterbury, the religious capital, which submitted in late October. He then swung west and north around London, ravaging Surrey and Hampshire to demonstrate the cost of resistance, before crossing the Thames at Wallingford. The strategy was not to assault London but to circle it, cut its supply lines and let the leaders inside come to him.

Key Fact

Between mid-October and December 1066, William circled London via Romney, Dover, Canterbury, Wallingford and Berkhamsted. He did not need to storm the capital — the encirclement and his ravaging of the surrounding shires forced the city’s leaders to come out and submit.

The Witan’s Last Throw: Edgar Atheling

Inside London the surviving Witan briefly elected the teenage Edgar Atheling king. He was the last male of the West Saxon line and the only candidate left with royal blood. But he had no army. The northern earls Edwin and Morcar had already returned to their earldoms. Archbishop Stigand of Canterbury and Archbishop Ealdred of York could not raise the city to fight. By early December, with William’s army at Berkhamsted just 30 miles north of London, the leading bishops, Edgar himself, and Edwin and Morcar rode out and submitted to William, offering the crown.

Berkhamsted was the moment the conquest passed from military victory to political legitimacy. The men who came out to submit included the two leading archbishops in England and the king-elect Edgar himself. Their submission meant that William’s coronation, when it came, would be performed by Anglo-Saxon clergy, witnessed by Anglo-Saxon nobles, and presented as a continuation of the kingship of Edward the Confessor — not as a foreign takeover.

The Coronation, Christmas Day 1066

William was crowned at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066, ten weeks after Hastings and on the spot where Harold had been crowned the year before. Archbishop Ealdred of York performed the consecration; Stigand was passed over because his pallium (a vestment of office) had come from a disputed pope and his position was insecure. The ceremony followed the Anglo-Saxon coronation order, with the new king swearing to defend the Church, govern justly and uphold the laws of his predecessors.

Outside the abbey something went badly wrong. When the congregation shouted out their assent, in both English and Norman French, the Norman guards stationed around the building thought a riot had broken out. They set fire to the surrounding houses to disperse the crowd. According to the Norman chronicler Orderic Vitalis, the church emptied as people ran out to fight the flames or save their property; only the bishops and a few clergy stayed to finish the ceremony. William was visibly shaken — an early sign that conciliation and force would have to run side by side.

William’s early policies were deliberately moderate. He confirmed Anglo-Saxon law and the rights of London in a charter to the citizens of London, written in English. He kept English bishops in their sees, including Stigand for now. Edwin and Morcar retained their earldoms, on terms. Several English thegns were allowed to keep their lands in return for renewed oaths. Conciliation was a tool of conquest: it bought time while William consolidated, built castles and brought over Norman lords. The harder line came later, after the revolts of 1067–71.

Castles: The First Tools of Control

Even as William was crowned, his men were building. The first motte-and-bailey castles went up in London, Dover, Canterbury, Winchester and Wallingford within months of Hastings. Each was a small wooden tower on an earth mound with a fenced courtyard. They could be thrown up in a few weeks using forced English labour and a small Norman garrison. Their function was to project Norman power into a town and dominate its markets, river crossings and roads. They were instruments of conquest first and defensive structures second — a misconception worth correcting in any answer about Norman control.

Key Fact

By spring 1067 motte-and-bailey castles dominated London (the future Tower), Dover, Canterbury and other major towns. They were instruments of conquest — projection of Norman power into the heart of English civilian life — not just border defences.

What Coronation Did Not Mean

Coronation gave William legal title across the kingdom, but real control was thin. The Midlands, the North and the Welsh borderlands had submitted in writing only. Many shires had never seen a Norman soldier. William sailed back to Normandy in March 1067 with English hostages and treasure, leaving his half-brother Odo of Bayeux and William FitzOsbern as regents. Within months a wave of revolts would test how thin Norman control really was — the subject of the next lesson.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of William’s march from Hastings to London in late 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William moved east along the coast first, taking Romney and Dover, before turning inland to Canterbury — using submissions rather than pitched battle to extend his control.
• Rather than assault London directly, William circled the city via Wallingford and Berkhamsted, ravaging Surrey and Hampshire to force the leaders inside to come out and submit.
• Norman troops fortified key points along the route, including Dover Castle within eight days of arrival, projecting Norman power into the local landscape.
• The march ended at Berkhamsted where Edgar Atheling, Edwin, Morcar and the leading bishops submitted and offered William the crown.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of William’s coronation at Westminster Abbey on 25 December 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It gave William legal title to the throne under Anglo-Saxon ritual: he was anointed by Archbishop Ealdred of York and presented as Edward the Confessor’s lawful successor, not a foreign conqueror.
• It bound the surviving English bishops and nobles to him through their participation in the ceremony, making future resistance look like rebellion against a crowned king rather than national defence.
• The riot outside the abbey, when Norman guards burned the surrounding houses after mistaking the congregation’s shout for an attack, showed the fragility of consent and prefigured the harder Norman line later.
• Coronation released William to leave for Normandy in March 1067, since he could now appoint regents and govern at a distance — a freedom uncrowned conquest would not have given him.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of early Norman motte-and-bailey castles.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• A motte was an artificial earth mound, often 5 to 10 metres high, topped by a wooden tower (the keep) where the Norman lord and his small garrison lived.
• A bailey was the fenced courtyard at the base of the motte, holding stables, storerooms, a hall and quarters for soldiers, surrounded by a ditch and palisade.
• Castles could be thrown up in weeks using forced English labour and prefabricated timber sections William had brought from Normandy.
• They were placed in occupied towns and at river crossings — for example in London (the future Tower), Dover, Canterbury and Winchester — to project Norman power into civilian life, not just to defend borders.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of William’s early policy of conciliation between October 1066 and spring 1067.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Confirming Anglo-Saxon law and the rights of London in a charter written in English allowed William to claim continuity with Edward the Confessor’s rule and reduced the case for revolt.
• Keeping English bishops, including Archbishop Stigand for the time being, helped the regime function: the Church administered baptisms, courts and charitable provision that an alien clergy could not have run alone.
• Letting Edwin and Morcar retain their earldoms (on renewed oaths) bought time while William imported Norman lords gradually rather than triggering a unified national revolt.
• The policy was a tool, not a settlement: when revolts began in 1067–68, William increasingly removed English nobles and replaced them with Normans — the harsher policy of the next phase only worked because conciliation had bought him 18 months of stability first.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Edgar Atheling’s submission at Berkhamsted in December 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Edgar’s submission removed the only blood-line claimant capable of rallying the Witan against William; without him, no rival coronation was possible.
• It was performed alongside Edwin, Morcar and the leading bishops, which gave William’s coronation broad Anglo-Saxon endorsement — significance lay in who submitted, not just that someone did.
• Significance over time: Edgar became a recurring figurehead for revolts — the 1068 northern revolt, the 1069 Danish-backed revolt — showing that submission did not equal loyalty.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from October–December 1066, that William’s political skill — rather than military force alone — turned the victory at Hastings into a successful conquest.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The decision to circle London via Wallingford and Berkhamsted rather than assault it traded slow encirclement for negotiated submission, sparing the army a costly siege.
• Using Anglo-Saxon coronation ritual at Westminster Abbey, performed by Archbishop Ealdred of York, framed the new regime as a continuation of Edward’s kingship rather than a foreign takeover.
• Confirming Anglo-Saxon law and the rights of London in a charter to the citizens reassured the city’s elite that conquest did not mean dispossession — in the short term.
• Allowing Edwin and Morcar to keep their earldoms and Stigand to keep his see bought 18 months of stability that pure force would not have produced.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Hastings itself was a military victory; without it no political settlement was possible.
• Ravaging Surrey and Hampshire and the threat of further violence at Berkhamsted were forms of military pressure that compelled the political submission.
• Motte-and-bailey castles in London, Dover and Canterbury were a military investment from the start, not a political gesture — their purpose was projection of armed power into towns.
• The riot at the coronation showed how thin consent really was, suggesting force was always the underlying guarantor.

A strong response weighs political skill against military force and reaches a substantiated overall judgement.

before.description: Five years of revolt — Kent, Exeter, the North, Ely — that nearly unmade.
before.content_html:
Conquest Was Not Settled in 1066

William sailed back to Normandy in March 1067 with English hostages and treasure, leaving his half-brother Odo of Bayeux and William FitzOsbern as regents. Within months, large parts of the country were in revolt. Between 1067 and 1071 William fought four major risings — in Kent, Exeter, the North, and the Fens — and in 1075 a fifth, the Earls’ Revolt. Each one nearly unmade the conquest. The misconception that Anglo-Saxon resistance was uncoordinated and doomed underestimates how close William came to defeat in 1069.

Kent and Eustace of Boulogne, 1067

The first revolt came on the very coast where William had landed. Eustace of Boulogne, a former ally now alienated by Odo’s rule in Kent, attempted a surprise attack on Dover Castle in autumn 1067. Local English thegns supported him, hoping a successful raid would chase the Normans out. The attack failed: the small Norman garrison held the castle on its high cliff, and Eustace withdrew. The episode showed two things — that the Normans’ new castles worked, and that resistance was already pulling in foreign allies as well as English rebels.

Exeter, 1068

In early 1068 Exeter, the largest town in the south-west, refused to pay an increased tribute and to admit a Norman garrison. The town was defended by Roman walls and the surviving Godwin family, including Harold’s mother Gytha. William marched in person with an army that included an English contingent — the first time the new king had used native English troops. The siege lasted 18 days. When Exeter surrendered, William showed measured terms: the city walls were left intact, no general massacre, but a new motte-and-bailey castle — Rougemont — was raised inside the walls to dominate the town. Gytha fled abroad.

Key Fact

Between 1067 and 1071 William faced four major revolts: Kent (Eustace of Boulogne, 1067), Exeter (the south-west, 1068), the North (Edwin and Morcar, then a Danish-backed rising in 1069), and Ely (Hereward and the Fens, 1070–71). Each was met with a new castle or worse.

Edwin, Morcar and the First Northern Revolt, 1068

Later in 1068 the northern earls Edwin of Mercia and Morcar of Northumbria revolted. They had submitted at Berkhamsted in 1066 and kept their earldoms, but they had been sidelined: Norman lords were taking land in their territories, and Edwin’s expected marriage to William’s daughter had not happened. They were joined by Edgar Atheling, who had fled north. William marched up the Roman road, building castles at Warwick, Nottingham, York and Lincoln as he went. The mere appearance of the army was enough; Edwin and Morcar submitted again, Edgar fled to Scotland, and the revolt collapsed without a battle. The lesson William took was that the North needed permanent garrisons.

The Second Northern Revolt and the Danish Fleet, 1069

The most dangerous moment of William’s reign came in 1069. In January, Robert de Comines, the new Norman earl of Northumbria, was killed in Durham along with around 700 of his men. In September a Danish fleet of around 240 ships under Sweyn II of Denmark, supporting the English claim of Edgar Atheling, sailed up the Humber. They were joined by the northern earls and by Anglo-Saxon nobles from Yorkshire and beyond. The combined force stormed York in late September; the Norman garrison was wiped out and the city’s castles destroyed. For a few weeks in autumn 1069, with revolts also flaring in Devon, Cornwall and the Welsh Marches, William’s rule was genuinely on the line.

The 1069 northern revolt combined a foreign invasion fleet, the legitimate Anglo-Saxon claimant Edgar Atheling, and the regional nobility of the North all at once. Norman chronicler Orderic Vitalis records William reportedly saying he would ‘not lay down his arms until I have brought the rebels to such submission as they shall never forget’. He bought off the Danish fleet with a payment to leave, then turned on the rebels. The decision to crush the North in winter 1069–70 — the Harrying — came directly out of how dangerous this revolt had been.

Hereward and the Isle of Ely, 1070–71

The last major revolt of the conquest period was based in the marshes of the Fens. Hereward, a Lincolnshire thegn whose lands had been confiscated, used the Isle of Ely — a chunk of dry ground surrounded by miles of marsh — as a base for raids. He was joined by another Danish fleet briefly in 1070, by Earl Morcar (now in revolt for the second time), and by other dispossessed thegns. William attacked the Isle in 1071 by building causeways across the marshes; one collapsed under the weight of his army, drowning many men. Eventually the rebels were betrayed by the monks of Ely, who feared further reprisals. Morcar was captured and imprisoned for life. Hereward escaped into legend, his story exaggerated by later medieval ballads.

Castles as the Answer to Revolt

Each revolt left a trail of castles in its wake. After Exeter came Rougemont; after the 1068 northern revolt came castles at Warwick, Nottingham, York and Lincoln; after 1069 came rebuilt double castles at York and stronger garrisons across the North. By 1100, around 500 castles had been built across England — an extraordinary density compared to Anglo-Saxon defences. The pattern is clear: William responded to revolt with permanent military infrastructure designed to make a repeat impossible. Castles were a direct strategic response to resistance, not a generic feature of Norman culture.

The early conciliation policy of 1066–67 collapsed under the strain of repeated revolt. After 1068 William increasingly removed English nobles, replaced them with Normans, and centralised land in the hands of a few tenants-in-chief such as Robert of Mortain, William FitzOsbern and Odo of Bayeux. Castle-building, harsher punishments and the dispossession of Anglo-Saxon thegns went together; revolt was the trigger.

Key Fact

The 1069 northern revolt combined a Danish invasion fleet of about 240 ships with the Anglo-Saxon claim of Edgar Atheling and risings across Devon, Cornwall and the Welsh Marches. William bought off the Danes, then turned to the harrying campaign — an answer extreme enough to ensure no comparable revolt happened again under William I.

An Anglo-Saxon nobleman of the second rank below an earl; a landholding warrior who served the king and dominated local society.
The greatest Norman lords who held their lands directly from the king in return for military service, forming the top tier of the post-conquest feudal system.

Examiners reward causal links between specific events and specific policies, not lists.

before.content_html:
A Reign-Defining Decision

By December 1069 William had bought off the Danish fleet and recaptured York, but the autumn revolt had been the most dangerous moment of his reign. He decided that mercy and conciliation had failed in the North. Through the winter of 1069 to 1070 his army moved across Yorkshire, Durham and beyond in a deliberate campaign of destruction known to historians as the Harrying of the North. The misconception students fall into is that ‘100,000 dead’ is a hard fact. It is a chronicle figure written more than fifty years later. What the Harrying actually was — and how brutal — is a debate active among historians today.

What William Did

William divided his army into smaller mobile bands and sent them out from a base at York. These detachments burned villages, slaughtered livestock and destroyed grain stores and farming tools wherever they went. The campaign focused on Yorkshire but reached into Durham, Cheshire and the Tees valley. It deliberately ran through winter, when food was scarcest and rebuilding was slowest. Survivors who escaped the raids faced famine; the chroniclers describe people eating dogs, horses and even, in shocked passages, each other.

Key Fact

The Harrying of the North took place in the winter of 1069–70. Yorkshire was hit hardest, with Durham, Cheshire and the Tees valley also devastated. Villages, livestock and food stores were destroyed deliberately to make rebellion impossible.

The Chroniclers’ Voice: Orderic and John of Worcester

Most of what we know about the Harrying comes from two later monastic writers. The Norman chronicler Orderic Vitalis wrote his Ecclesiastical History around 1125, more than fifty years after the events. Although he served a Norman abbey, he condemned William’s decision in unusually strong language: ‘In his anger he commanded that all crops and herds, chattels and food of every kind should be brought together and burned to ashes.’ Orderic went on to claim that more than 100,000 people died of hunger in the months that followed and that William had committed an unforgivable crime against the innocent. John of Worcester, writing slightly earlier, gives a similar picture of mass starvation and depopulation across the North.

The Domesday ‘Waste’ Entries

When the Domesday commissioners reached Yorkshire in 1086, they recorded enormous numbers of villages with the Latin entry vasta est, ‘it is waste’. In some districts more than half the recorded settlements were marked waste, sixteen years after the Harrying. For older historians this was direct numerical proof of catastrophic destruction — whole regions wiped clean. The political effect is undisputed: large-scale revolt against William I never happened in the North again.

More recent work has cautioned against reading every ‘waste’ entry as proof of physical destruction. A village might be ‘waste’ because it had no taxable value at the moment of survey, because tenants had fled, because the lord could not produce records, or because the estate had been deliberately reorganised by Norman tenants-in-chief. Some ‘waste’ districts are far enough from the documented Harrying route that they cannot easily be blamed on William’s soldiers. The destruction was real, but the Domesday data is fiscal as much as it is forensic.

Modern Historiography: How Bad, How Big?

Modern historians sit between two earlier extremes. Older nineteenth- and twentieth-century scholarship took Orderic’s 100,000 dead largely at face value and called the Harrying a genocide. More recent work, including Hugh Thomas’s The English and the Normans (2003), reads it as catastrophic but smaller in scale than Orderic claimed — the figure inflated by a writer working in a tradition that condemned cruelty in princes. What no historian now denies is the political effect: terror that ended the threat of large-scale northern revolt for the rest of William I’s reign.

A high-band answer does not just repeat ‘100,000 dead’. It explains where the figure comes from (Orderic, c.1125), notes that it is a chronicle estimate written decades after the events by a writer hostile to royal cruelty, and weighs it against the Domesday ‘waste’ pattern of 1086. The point is not to dismiss the suffering — it was real and unprecedented — but to handle the evidence carefully, as the AQA mark schemes and examiner reports consistently reward.

Long-Term Effect on Northern Landholding

The Harrying changed the map of northern landholding. Many Anglo-Saxon thegns who survived had no estates left to hold; their lands were redistributed to a small group of trusted Normans who would now garrison the North. The North-east was reorganised under figures such as the bishop of Durham and Alan Rufus of Richmond, who built castles to hold their new territories. By 1086, Yorkshire was one of the most thoroughly Normanised regions of England despite having been the most rebellious in 1069. That is the reign-defining trade William made in the winter of 1069–70.

Key Fact

Orderic Vitalis wrote about the Harrying around 1125, more than fifty years after the events. His figure of 100,000 dead is treated by modern historians as evidence of perceived horror rather than a precise head-count, and Domesday ‘waste’ entries can have many causes besides direct destruction.

glossary_terms.definition: William’s deliberate winter campaign of 1069–70 across northern England, designed to crush rebellion by destroying villages, livestock and food stores.
An Anglo-Norman monk and historian (1075–c.1142) of the abbey of St Evroul, whose Ecclesiastical History is a major source for the Norman Conquest, written about fifty years after the events.
An English monk (d. 1140) at Worcester Priory whose Latin chronicle of English history is one of the main contemporary sources for William’s reign and the Harrying.
A Domesday Book entry meaning ‘wasted’ or worthless — villages or estates with no taxable value, often interpreted as showing destruction or depopulation.

before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on the Harrying, separate significance at the time from significance over time. At the time, the Harrying ended the 1069 revolt and bought off any repeat. Over time, it reshaped northern landholding, planted a network of new Norman lords and castles, and gave William the historical reputation that Anglo-Norman chroniclers themselves struggled with. Examiners reward students who weigh both moments and use historians’ treatment of the chronicle evidence rather than repeating ‘100,000 dead’ as fact.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of William’s Harrying of the North in the winter of 1069 to 1070.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• It was a deliberate winter campaign — William divided his army into mobile detachments based at York and sent them out across Yorkshire and beyond when food was scarcest and rebuilding hardest.
• Villages were burned, livestock slaughtered and grain stores and farming tools destroyed, leaving survivors to face famine through the winter and into the spring of 1070.
• Northern regions affected included Yorkshire (worst hit), Durham, Cheshire and the Tees valley — not a single concentrated battle but a months-long sweep across roughly two hundred miles.
• Chroniclers such as Orderic Vitalis described mass starvation in the months that followed, with people reduced to eating dogs, horses and worse.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Harrying of the North in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the Harrying ended the 1069 northern revolt by destroying the regional resource base — villages, livestock and food stores — on which any future rising would have depended.
• It deterred further northern revolt under William I; the political effect is undisputed even when historians disagree about scale.
• Over time, it allowed wholesale redistribution of northern land to trusted Norman lords such as Alan Rufus at Richmond and the bishop of Durham, who garrisoned the North with new castles.
• Significance is also moral and historiographical: even Norman chroniclers like Orderic Vitalis condemned the campaign, and it has shaped William’s reputation among historians for nine centuries.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples and careful use of chronicle evidence.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of contemporary chronicle evidence for the Harrying of the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Orderic Vitalis, a Norman monk at St Evroul writing his Ecclesiastical History around 1125 — more than fifty years after the events — condemned William and gave the figure of 100,000 dead in famine after the campaign.
• John of Worcester, an English monk writing earlier in the 12th century, gives a comparable picture of mass starvation and depopulation across northern England.
• Both writers worked decades after the Harrying using earlier sources and oral tradition, which explains why historians treat their numerical claims with caution.
• Both also show the unusual fact that even Norman-aligned writers were prepared to criticise William for this episode, suggesting the brutality was striking even by 11th-century standards.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Harrying of the North on landholding in Yorkshire and the North-east.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Many Anglo-Saxon thegns who survived had no estates left to defend, accelerating the dispossession recorded later in Domesday Book where fewer than 10% of pre-conquest landholders still held land in 1086.
• Northern lands were granted to a small group of trusted Normans — Alan Rufus received the great honour of Richmond, the bishop of Durham was given vast estates — concentrating power in a few loyal hands.
• These new lords planted castles to hold the redistributed estates, weaving the network of motte-and-bailey strongpoints that anchored the North through the 12th century.
• Domesday’s 1086 entries of vasta est (waste) record a depressed taxable value across much of Yorkshire even sixteen years later — though historians caution that ‘waste’ can also reflect tenant flight or administrative reorganisation.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and clear causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of historians’ debate about the scale of the Harrying for understanding Norman rule.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the brutality was so striking that even Norman writers like Orderic Vitalis condemned William — the contemporary unease is itself historical evidence about how harsh the campaign was perceived to be.
• Modern historians such as Hugh Thomas (2003) read Orderic’s 100,000 figure as inflated by genre conventions and decades of distance, but agree the destruction was unprecedented in scale — the debate refines, rather than removes, the seriousness of the Harrying.
• Domesday ‘waste’ entries can be read as fiscal records of low taxable value as well as physical destruction, so the 1086 evidence requires careful handling rather than direct quotation.
• Significance over time: how we judge the Harrying shapes how we judge Norman rule overall — whether the conquest was a measured takeover with continuity beneath (Hugh Thomas) or a violent rupture (Marc Morris).

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples and named historians.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that the Harrying of the North was the decisive turning point in Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The Harrying ended the most dangerous revolt of William’s reign — the 1069 Danish-backed northern rising that had stormed York and threatened simultaneous risings in Devon, Cornwall and the Welsh Marches.
• It cleared the way for wholesale redistribution of northern land to a small group of Norman tenants-in-chief and the castle network that anchored their lordships.
• The political effect was permanent: large-scale revolt against William I did not happen again in the North after 1070, even when revolt flared in 1075 and 1088 elsewhere.
• It marked the end of William’s conciliatory phase; from 1070 onward Anglo-Saxon nobles were systematically dispossessed and the Norman aristocracy was consolidated.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Hastings (1066) was the indispensable battlefield victory — without it there would have been no conquest to defend.
• The 1067–71 revolts as a whole, not just the northern revolt, drove the shift from conciliation to occupation; the Earls’ Revolt of 1075 and the 1088 rebellion against William II show consolidation continued long after the Harrying.
• Domesday Book (1086) and the redistribution it records represent a separate, longer process of administrative and tenurial settlement.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms from 1070 transformed the Norman hold on personnel and ideology in ways the Harrying alone did not.

A strong response weighs the Harrying against military victory, the wider revolts and longer-term institutional change, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Feudalism and the Norman Land Settlement

before.content_html:
A Working Pyramid, Not a Blueprint

Students often imagine William sitting down with a chart and inventing a ‘feudal system’. The reality is messier. The pattern of feudalism was a working set of landholding-for-service relationships that had developed in northern France over the previous century, and William transplanted it to England after 1066. He did not build it from scratch; he intensified what Norman lords already knew. The historian Susan Reynolds (1994) has even argued that calling feudalism a ‘system’ flatters its tidiness — what existed was a set of overlapping working relationships. AQA still teaches the model because students need a framework, but examiner reports reward those who can describe the real military and land obligations rather than chant a textbook hierarchy.

King at the Top

After 1066 William claimed all the land of England as his by right of conquest. He kept some — the royal demesne — for himself, including key forests, castles and towns, and granted the rest out to followers in return for service. The principle that all land was ultimately the king’s was a sharper Norman idea than anything in pre-1066 England, where great Anglo-Saxon earls had held land in their own right. By 1086, every estate in England traced back to the king through a chain of holders.

Key Fact

The Norman pyramid had four levels: the king at the top, around 180 tenants-in-chief who held land directly from him, sub-tenants (often knights) who held from those, and at the bottom the peasants — mostly Anglo-Saxon — who worked the land. Land was held in return for specified service.

Tenants-in-Chief

Beneath the king sat the tenants-in-chief: the great Norman lords who held estates directly from William and owed him counsel and military service. Domesday Book records around 180 of them. The biggest holdings went to William’s closest family and supporters — his half-brothers Odo of Bayeux and Robert of Mortain, his loyal commander William FitzOsbern, and a handful of others. Robert of Mortain alone held nearly 800 manors across thirteen counties; Odo of Bayeux was lord of vast estates centred on Kent. A relatively small group of men therefore held a remarkably large share of the kingdom — a deliberate concentration of military power in trusted hands.

Sub-Tenants and Knights’ Fees

Tenants-in-chief in turn granted out portions of their estates to followers in a process called sub-infeudation. The unit of grant was the knight’s fee — an estate large enough to support a fully equipped knight and his household. In return the sub-tenant owed a fixed amount of military service, typically forty days a year. A great honour like Robert of Mortain’s might be sub-divided into dozens or hundreds of knights’ fees, which is how England’s small Norman ruling class managed to put thousands of armed knights into the field on demand.

Land was the currency of loyalty. A king who could grant a knight’s fee, a manor or a great honour created a personal bond — the holder owed loyalty for what he held. The flow of patronage ran down the pyramid: the king rewarded tenants-in-chief, who rewarded their own knights. When patronage broke down — as in the 1075 Earls’ Revolt or the 1088 rising against William II — the system shook because the chain of obligation snapped at one of its links.

Peasants at the Base

The vast majority of people in England were peasants who worked the land. Domesday lists several categories: villeins (owing labour service to their lord), bordars and cottars (smaller holdings), freemen, and slaves — perhaps 10% of the population in 1086, although slavery was already declining. For most peasants, the conquest changed the language and name of the lord at the top of their manor, but daily labour patterns continued. They still ploughed the same strips, paid the same kinds of dues, and lived in the same villages. The novelty was the Norman lord on the hill.

The Anglo-Saxon Aristocracy Replaced

For the Anglo-Saxon landholding class — the thegns — the conquest was catastrophic. Domesday Book shows that by 1086 fewer than 10% of pre-conquest landholders still held land. The rest had been killed in the campaigns of 1066–71, exiled, or reduced to tenants of Norman incomers. The thegnage as a class effectively vanished within a generation. Where they survived, surviving thegns held smaller estates as sub-tenants of Norman lords — a sharp social demotion.

Robert of Mortain was William’s half-brother. Domesday records him holding nearly 800 manors across thirteen counties, including coastal estates in Sussex and vast lands in Cornwall. He sub-infeudated dozens of his manors to his own knights, who held by knight-service. The pattern is typical of the new tenants-in-chief: huge holdings, multiple shires, a private network of sub-tenants who answered to Robert before they answered to the king. Such concentrations of land made conquest stick, but they also created the political muscle behind later rebellions, including the 1088 rising in which Robert of Mortain himself took part.

A Coalition, Not One Group

Another misconception students fall into is treating ‘the Normans’ as one homogeneous people. William’s invasion army was a coalition: Normans, Bretons, Flemings and French. His post-conquest aristocracy reflected that mix — Bretons such as Alan Rufus held the honour of Richmond; Flemings settled in the south; tenants-in-chief came from across northern France and the Low Countries. Calling everyone ‘Norman’ obscures the patronage politics that William had to manage at the top of the pyramid.

Key Fact

By 1086, fewer than 10% of pre-conquest English landholders still held land. The Anglo-Saxon thegnage was effectively replaced as a class within twenty years — either dispossessed, killed, exiled or reduced to sub-tenants of Norman lords.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of sub-infeudation in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:

• It enabled rapid response to revolt: a tenant-in-chief could call up dozens or hundreds of knights for forty-day service from his sub-tenants, the system that produced the armies that crushed the 1067–71 risings.
• Significance over time: sub-infeudation became the template for English landholding through the 12th and 13th centuries, recorded in feudal aids and survey records like the Cartae Baronum (1166).

lessons.title: Castles: Instruments of Conquest and Control

before.content_html:
A Kingdom Held Down by Earthworks

In 1066 there were perhaps fifty castles in the whole of England. By 1100 there were close to five hundred. The Normans were a tiny ruling minority — perhaps 8,000 fighting men sitting on top of two million Anglo-Saxons — and the castle was the technology that made that imbalance work. To understand Norman control, you have to understand the castle as an instrument of conquest first and a defensive structure second.

Why England Had So Few Castles Before 1066

Anglo-Saxon England did not build castles in the Norman sense. Local defence rested on burhs — communal fortified towns first developed under King Alfred against Viking raids. Burhs protected whole communities. Castles, by contrast, were private fortresses owned by individual lords. The few pre-conquest castles in England (such as those built by Edward the Confessor’s Norman favourites in Herefordshire) were resented by the English precisely because they looked foreign and threatening — they pointed inward at the local population, not outward at invaders.

Key Fact

The number of castles in England rose from about fifty in 1066 to roughly five hundred by 1100. This explosion of building was the physical infrastructure of the Norman Conquest.

Motte-and-Bailey: Speed Over Strength

The most common Norman castle was the motte-and-bailey. The motte was a steep earth mound, sometimes natural and shaped, sometimes built up from scratch using forced English labour. On top sat a wooden tower — the lord’s residence and final stronghold. Beside the motte lay the bailey, a flat enclosed courtyard surrounded by a ditch and a palisade of sharpened timbers, holding stables, kitchens, a chapel, a hall and quarters for the garrison.

The point of the motte-and-bailey was speed. A wooden castle could be thrown up in a fortnight using local labour. William ordered one built at Hastings within hours of landing, using prefabricated timbers brought from Normandy. After his coronation he marched through southern England building motte-and-baileys at strategic points; after the rebellions of 1067–71 he flooded the disturbed areas with new ones.

Motte-and-bailey design had developed in northern France in the tenth and early eleventh centuries, where rival lords needed cheap, defensible bases during the long break-up of Carolingian authority. By 1066 it was the standard Norman tool of lordship. William’s army arrived already trained in throwing them up. The Bayeux Tapestry shows English labourers being driven by Norman overseers to dig the motte at Hastings — one of the few visual records of a castle being built.

Stone Keeps: Permanence and Statement

Wood rotted, burned and could be chopped down. Where William wanted permanence — especially in major cities and royal centres — he replaced timber with stone. The greatest example is the White Tower, begun in the 1070s on the eastern edge of London. Its walls are over four metres thick at the base. Its scale was meant to be visible from the river: any merchant or rebel arriving at the capital saw a Norman fortress before they saw the city.

Other stone keeps followed at Colchester (built directly over the ruins of the Roman temple of Claudius, deliberately reusing imperial stonework), at Lincoln, and at Rochester. Stone construction was slow and expensive — only the king and the wealthiest tenants-in-chief could afford it. By 1100, stone keeps remained the exception; most of the c.500 castles in England were still timber on earth.

Siting: Roads, Rivers and Rebels

Where you put a castle decided what it could do. Norman lords sited castles to control river crossings (Wallingford on the Thames, Cambridge on the Cam), road junctions (Berkhamsted on the route from London to the Midlands), the entrances to towns (York, Lincoln, Nottingham — sometimes two castles per town, on opposite banks), and rebellious regions (the lordships of the Welsh Marches, where Hereford, Shrewsbury and Chester anchored a frontier line).

Key Fact

Norman castles were sited to control three things: movement (rivers, roads, town gates), people (rebellious regions, urban populations) and patronage networks (the centre of a tenant-in-chief’s landholdings). Defence against invasion was rarely the first reason.

Castles as Instruments of Power

It is tempting to see castles as defensive shells — places to retreat into when attacked. They were, but only secondarily. Their primary function was projection: a permanent garrison of armed Norman knights stationed in the middle of an English town or shire, riding out to enforce lordship, collect rents, hold courts and intimidate the locals. Building one often meant demolishing English houses; castle-work meant forcing English peasants to dig the ditches and raise the motte without pay.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, written by English monks, captures this resentment with bitter clarity. Castles, the Chronicler complained, ‘filled the country’ and gave the Norman lords a base from which to oppress the English with taxes and labour. The very visibility of a motte rising over a market square was the message: this land has new owners, and they live on a hill watching you.

Berkhamsted — a motte-and-bailey on the road from London to the Midlands, built shortly after Hastings; the Witan submitted to William here in December 1066. York — two motte-and-baileys on opposite banks of the Ouse, built after the 1069 northern revolt to anchor the Harrying. Lincoln — built on the highest point in the city after 166 English houses were demolished to make room. Tower of London — the White Tower in stone, dominating the river approach to the capital.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The number of castles in England rose from c.50 in 1066 to c.500 by 1100; this physical building programme was the infrastructure of the conquest.
  • Motte-and-bailey castles could be built in days using forced English labour; stone keeps such as the White Tower were rarer, slower and reserved for major royal centres.
  • Castles were instruments of power first and defensive structures second — sited to control river crossings, towns and rebellious regions and resented by the English as visible symbols of Norman dominance.
