before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘Describe Two Features’ question, the examiner wants two precise features plus a developed sentence of detail on each — not a list of four labels. A ‘feature’ could be motte-and-bailey design (with the developed detail of speed of construction) or stone keeps (with the example of the White Tower). Vague phrases like ‘they were used for defence’ score nothing because they apply to almost any castle in history.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of motte-and-bailey castles in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The motte was a raised earth mound, sometimes shaped from a natural rise and sometimes built up from scratch using forced English labour, with a wooden tower on top serving as the lord’s residence and final stronghold.
• The bailey was a flat enclosed courtyard beside the motte, surrounded by a ditch and timber palisade, holding the hall, chapel, stables and quarters for the Norman garrison.
• Motte-and-baileys could be built in a fortnight or less using local timber and conscripted labour, which made them the Normans’ tool of choice for rapid colonisation.
• They were sited at strategic points such as river crossings, road junctions and town entrances rather than purely defensive positions.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for a brief identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail.]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of stone castles built in England between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• They had massive walls, sometimes over four metres thick at the base, as at the White Tower of London begun in the 1070s.
• They were built at major royal and urban centres — the White Tower at London, Colchester reusing Roman stonework, Lincoln, Rochester — rather than at every minor lordship.
• Construction was slow and expensive, so only the king and the wealthiest tenants-in-chief could afford to build in stone; most castles by 1100 were still timber on earth.
• Stone keeps doubled as administrative centres and royal residences, projecting permanence and Norman authority over the city below.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for a developed feature with supporting detail.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of castle-building on Anglo-Saxon towns and villages between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Whole streets of English houses were demolished to clear ground for castles — at Lincoln, 166 houses were pulled down to make room for the new motte and bailey.
• Local English peasants were forced to dig ditches, raise mottes and cut timber under the labour duty of castle-work, draining the agricultural workforce during building seasons.
• Castle garrisons of Norman knights gave lords a permanent base from which to ride out, collect rents, hold private courts and intimidate the surrounding population.
• The visibility of a motte over a market square stamped Norman authority on every shire town — an effect that the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records as bitter resentment among the English.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with specific examples and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of motte-and-bailey castles for the Norman Conquest of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, motte-and-baileys allowed William’s small army (perhaps 8,000 fighting men) to plant a network of strongholds across a kingdom of two million people, beginning within hours of landing at Hastings.
• The speed of construction (a fortnight or less) meant the Normans could respond to revolt by flooding disturbed areas with new castles — the response to the 1067–71 rebellions and the Harrying of the North.
• Significance over time: by 1100 there were roughly 500 castles, and the network they formed underpinned tenant-in-chief lordship throughout the twelfth century.
• They reshaped English geography: market towns, road junctions and county centres reorganised around the new fortresses, a pattern still visible in cities such as York, Lincoln and Cambridge.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Norman castle-siting policy on royal control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Castles built at river crossings (Wallingford, Cambridge) and road junctions (Berkhamsted) gave the Crown control over movement, trade routes and the ability to track armed bands.
• Two castles in towns such as York and Lincoln — on opposite banks of the river — ensured no rebel force could occupy a city without facing armed Norman garrisons from both sides.
• The Welsh Marches were anchored by lordships at Hereford, Shrewsbury and Chester, creating a fortified frontier that stabilised the western borderlands.
• Castles in former rebel zones such as Yorkshire after the Harrying gave the Crown a permanent armed presence and discouraged further revolt.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named places and a clear causal chain.
Secure: Two or more effects explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that castles were the most important reason William and his successors held on to England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The number of castles rose from c.50 to c.500 between 1066 and 1100 — a permanent armed Norman garrison in every shire which made revolt physically harder.
• Castles such as the White Tower of London projected royal authority over the capital and the kingdom’s economic centre.
• During the rebellions of 1067–71 and the Harrying of the North, new castle-building was William’s direct response to revolt and the means of preventing future ones.
• By 1100 castles structured tenant-in-chief lordship across the country — the basis of Norman political control.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The Battle of Hastings itself was won by cavalry and archery, not castles — without that military victory there would have been no conquest to consolidate.
• The Harrying of the North (1069–70) terrorised resistance into submission through deliberate destruction, not through castle garrisons alone.
• The redistribution of land to c.180 tenants-in-chief (recorded in Domesday) tied the new aristocracy to the Crown by reward, with castles being only one part of that bond.
• Norman government structures — the inherited shires, sheriffs and writs — allowed routine taxation and justice to function alongside military control.

A strong response weighs castles against military victory, terror, land redistribution and government, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Norman Government, Justice and the Anglo-Saxon Inheritance

before.content_html:
Continuity Beneath Rupture

A common misconception is that the Norman Conquest was a clean break in English government. It was not. William inherited one of the most administratively sophisticated monarchies in Europe, and he kept most of its machinery intact. He changed the personnel at the top — thegns out, Norman barons in — and added a few sharp innovations of his own. The historian Hugh Thomas calls this ‘continuity beneath rupture’: ruling-class transformation on top of substantial Anglo-Saxon stability underneath. Understanding what was kept and what was added is the way to answer the spec’s comparison questions cleanly.

What the Normans Inherited

By 1066 England was already divided into shires and hundreds — the framework that lasted, in modified form, into modern times. Each shire was supervised by a royal officer called the sheriff (Anglo-Saxon ‘shire-reeve’) who collected the king’s revenues, presided over the shire court and led the local militia. Communication ran through the writ — a short sealed Latin or Old English document by which the king sent instructions to his sheriffs. England had also developed a sophisticated system of cash taxation through the geld, originally raised to pay off Viking raiders.

Key Fact

The Normans kept the Anglo-Saxon framework of government largely intact: shires and hundreds, sheriffs as royal officers, the writ as the standard royal instruction, and the geld land tax. The framework continued; the personnel changed.

Anglo-Saxon and Norman Aristocracies Compared

The pre-1066 ruling class were the great earls and the thegns — landholders who provided counsel through the Witan. They held lands in their own right, often dispersed across many shires, and their power rested on family networks as well as royal favour. The Norman tenants-in-chief who replaced them held land formally from the king, owed forty days’ military service per knight’s fee, and operated through a tighter pyramid of patronage. Where Anglo-Saxon earls had been semi-independent regional powers, Norman tenants-in-chief were the king’s sworn men first.

What the Normans Added

William also bolted on his own innovations. The most striking was forest law: vast tracts of countryside were declared royal hunting reserves, with savage penalties — blinding, mutilation, sometimes execution — for poaching, taking firewood or clearing land. The New Forest in Hampshire was created by clearing villages of their inhabitants. Forest law existed alongside, not instead of, ordinary common law — royal officers called foresters policed it through their own courts.

Even sharper was the murdrum fine. If a Norman was found dead with no clear killer, the hundred where the body lay had to pay a heavy collective fine to the king. The hundred could only escape this fine by producing the murderer — or by proving the dead man was English, a process called ‘presentment of Englishry’. The murdrum fine assumed Norman lives were under permanent threat from a hostile Anglo-Saxon population, and made every English community responsible for protecting Norman incomers.

The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records William’s passion for hunting in unusually pointed language: he ‘loved the tall stags as if he were their father’, while peasants who took game went blind. The New Forest was created in Hampshire on land cleared of villages and farmland; many of the displaced communities were never resettled. Forest law remained one of the bitterest English grievances against Norman rule for the next century, and it only began to be rolled back under Magna Carta and the Charter of the Forest in the early 13th century.

Justice and the Legal System

Most ordinary disputes still went to the local hundred court or shire court that had existed before 1066. There was no professional judiciary in the modern sense; the sheriff or a hundred reeve presided. When evidence was unclear, the courts used trial by ordeal: the accused carried a hot iron a set distance, plunged an arm into boiling water, or was bound and thrown into a pool. The wound that healed cleanly meant innocence; one that festered, guilt. The Normans added trial by combat, a duel between accuser and accused (or paid champions) that imported a continental warrior practice into English courts.

Inheritance and the New Norman Pattern

Anglo-Saxon inheritance had often been partible — estates divided between sons. Normans favoured primogeniture: the eldest son inherited the lot. This kept knights’ fees and great honours intact across generations and was crucial to the long-term survival of the feudal pyramid. The cost was political: William’s younger sons inherited less than the eldest. When William I died in 1087, his eldest son Robert Curthose got Normandy, his second son William II got England — and the resulting tension fuelled the 1088 rebellion.

In The English and the Normans (2003), Hugh Thomas argues that beneath dramatic Norman rupture — battles, dispossession, castles — lay substantial Anglo-Saxon continuity. The shire and hundred courts kept meeting; sheriffs kept collecting revenue; villages kept their fields and churches. Marc Morris, by contrast, emphasises the violence of the change — thegns dispossessed, bishops replaced, the Harrying of the North. AQA examiners reward students who can hold both readings together: government structure largely continuous, government personnel and high politics violently new.

Key Fact

The two sharpest Norman additions to English government were forest law (royal hunting reserves with savage penalties) and the murdrum fine (collective punishment imposed on hundreds where a Norman was killed). Both protected the new ruling class from a hostile Anglo-Saxon majority.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘Two Ways Similar or Different’ question on Anglo-Saxon and Norman government, choose two clear contrasts and develop each. Examples: (1) Anglo-Saxon earls held land in their own right, whereas Norman tenants-in-chief held formally from the king on knight-service. (2) Both systems used shires and sheriffs, but the Normans added forest law and the murdrum fine. Examiners reward genuine differences (or genuine similarities) developed with named institutions, not vague labels like ‘the Normans changed government’.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Anglo-Saxon system of local government inherited by the Normans after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• England was divided into shires (counties), each supervised by a royal officer called the sheriff or shire-reeve who collected royal revenues and presided over the shire court.
• Below the shire sat the hundred — smaller units that met monthly in their own courts to handle local justice, theft, debt and minor violence.
• The king communicated with sheriffs and shire courts through writs — short sealed documents in Old English or Latin sent across the kingdom on royal business.
• A national land tax called the geld was assessed on shires and hundreds in ‘hides’ and collected as cash, originally to pay off Viking raiders.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon and Norman government were similar.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both used the shire as the basic unit of local government, with a royal officer (sheriff or shire-reeve) collecting revenues and presiding over the shire court.
• Both relied on the writ — short sealed royal documents — to communicate the king’s instructions to his officers across the kingdom.
• Both raised cash through the geld land tax, assessed in hides on shires and hundreds and collected by sheriffs.
• Both used trial by ordeal in serious criminal cases, with the courts reading physical outcomes as God’s judgement on innocence or guilt.
[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon and Norman government were different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Anglo-Saxon great earls held lands in their own right and were semi-independent regional powers, while Norman tenants-in-chief held land formally from the king on knight-service.
• The Normans added forest law — royal hunting reserves with savage penalties for poaching — which had no Anglo-Saxon equivalent.
• The Normans introduced the murdrum fine, a collective penalty on the hundred where a Norman was killed, designed to protect the new ruling class.
• Norman inheritance favoured primogeniture (eldest son takes the lot), in contrast to the partible inheritance often used in Anglo-Saxon families.
[4 marks — 2 marks per difference: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of forest law in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, forest law placed vast tracts of countryside under royal control, restricting English access to timber, game and grazing — the New Forest was created by clearing villages of their inhabitants in Hampshire.
• Penalties for poaching and clearing land were extreme — blinding, mutilation, sometimes execution — an unprecedented intrusion of royal power into ordinary peasant life.
• It generated significant royal income through fines collected by foresters in their own courts, separate from the ordinary common law system.
• Significance over time: forest law remained one of the bitterest English grievances against royal authority for over a century and was only rolled back by Magna Carta and the Charter of the Forest in 1217.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the murdrum fine for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the murdrum fine made every English hundred collectively responsible for the safety of Norman incomers, deterring revenge attacks on isolated knights, sheriffs and lords.
• It generated steady royal revenue from communities that could not produce a killer or prove the dead man was English (the ‘presentment of Englishry’).
• It marked a sharp legal divide between Norman and English subjects of the same king, reinforcing the ethnic dimension of post-conquest rule.
• Significance over time: the fine survived for more than a century until the 12th century, when intermarriage made it impossible to tell Normans and English apart and the procedure was effectively abandoned.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that the Norman Conquest brought more continuity than change to English government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The framework of shires, hundreds and sheriffs continued largely intact — the local machinery of revenue collection and justice was Anglo-Saxon in origin and Norman in personnel.
• The writ as the standard royal instruction continued; sealed royal letters in Old English (and increasingly Latin) carried Norman commands through inherited channels.
• The geld land tax, in ‘hides’ assessed on shires and hundreds, was kept and indeed re-used by William to fund campaigns and military service obligations.
• Most ordinary justice still happened in hundred and shire courts using ordeals; trial by combat was a Norman addition but the bulk of dispute resolution went on as before.
• Hugh Thomas’s ‘continuity beneath rupture’ thesis emphasises that beneath new Norman lords, English peasants ploughed the same fields and used the same courts.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The personnel of government changed almost completely — thegns dispossessed by 1086 (fewer than 10% surviving as landholders), Norman tenants-in-chief and bishops in their place.
• Forest law and the murdrum fine were genuinely new, creating royal hunting reserves and ethnic distinctions in justice unknown before 1066.
• Norman castles, sub-infeudation and knight-service reorganised the relationship between landholding and military obligation in ways inconsistent with the ‘continuity’ reading.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms, the Domesday survey itself and the central concentration of power in c.180 tenants-in-chief all suggest a sharper political change than the institutional continuity alone.

A strong response weighs continuity in framework against rupture in personnel and innovations like forest law and murdrum, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

Examiners reward students who handle ‘waste’ entries carefully rather than treating Domesday as a literal headcount.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Domesday survey of 1086.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• William ordered it at his Christmas court at Gloucester in 1085, and the survey was complete by August 1086 — less than nine months of fieldwork across 31 shires.
• Royal commissioners (typically a bishop, baron and clerk) travelled in circuits to each shire and questioned juries from the hundreds under oath, working from a fixed list of questions.
• For each manor the commissioners recorded the holder in 1066 and 1086, the value ‘then’ and ‘now’, the geld assessment in hides, ploughs, peasants and resources such as mills, fisheries and woodlands.
• The results were written up in Latin in two volumes — Great Domesday for most of England and Little Domesday for Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex — and stored in the royal treasury at Winchester.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Domesday Book in establishing Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Domesday gave William the data he needed to raise the geld accurately at a moment of military emergency — the threatened Danish invasion of 1085 had brought a mercenary army to England that had to be paid.
• It locked down the shape of the post-conquest aristocracy by recording around 180 tenants-in-chief and confirming who held what, by what right, from whom — the legal record of the Norman land settlement.
• It demonstrated royal authority by showing William knew, in writing, what every manor in his kingdom was worth — the 12th-century commentator Richard FitzNigel later said its findings could not be appealed.
• Significance over time: Domesday entries became the working baseline for every later royal taxation and legal claim throughout the medieval period, and the volume survives at the National Archives today.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the procedure used by the Domesday commissioners in 1086.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Commissioners worked from a fixed list of questions covering the holder in 1066 and 1086, the geld assessment in hides, ploughs, peasants and resources, and the value ‘then’ and ‘now’.
• Each circuit of commissioners was made up of a bishop, a baron and a clerk — men of high status whose seniority underwrote the authority of the survey.
• In each shire they sat in the shire court and questioned juries from the hundreds — panels of named English and Norman freemen sworn to give evidence on oath.
• Returns were written up in Latin and sent to royal clerks at Winchester, who compressed them into the per-shire entries of Great Domesday.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Christmas council at Gloucester in December 1085.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the council took place in the middle of an invasion crisis — Cnut IV of Denmark was preparing a fleet to claim the English throne, and William had brought a large mercenary army to England that had to be paid.
• William’s decision to commission a kingdom-wide survey at this moment shows that royal administration responded to military pressure with sharper data, not simply more troops.
• The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records William’s ‘deep speech’ with his council about how the country was occupied; the council marks the conversion of vague royal knowledge into systematic record.
• Significance over time: the decision produced Domesday Book itself, the working baseline of English royal administration for centuries to come.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Domesday survey on the Anglo-Saxon population of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• The survey confirmed in writing the dispossession of the Anglo-Saxon thegnage; fewer than 10% of pre-conquest English landholders still held land in 1086, with most lost to death, exile or demotion.
• Domesday recorded English peasants — villeins, bordars, cottars, freemen and slaves — with their numbers and obligations on each manor, fixing the working population in fiscal records under their new Norman lords.
• The geld assessments enabled more accurate royal taxation that drew cash from the rural population, intensifying the financial demands on Anglo-Saxon villages.
• In Yorkshire and Cheshire many villages were recorded as ‘waste’ (vasta est) — a fiscal label that captured the after-effects of the Harrying as well as later tenurial reorganisation, depressing the recorded value of the region for decades.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with precise examples.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

Note on careful evidence handling: high-band answers acknowledge that ‘waste’ in Domesday is fiscal data and not always a direct headcount of destruction.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that the Domesday Book was the most striking achievement of Norman government.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• In less than nine months, royal commissioners surveyed 31 shires, 13,000 settlements and over 268,000 named individuals — a feat of administrative reach unequalled in medieval Europe.
• The book locked down the post-conquest land settlement by recording around 180 tenants-in-chief and confirming who held what from the king — the legal record of the Norman aristocracy.
• Its tax data underpinned the royal finances during the 1085 invasion crisis and for decades afterwards, providing the geld base that paid armies and built castles.
• Significance over time: Domesday entries became the working baseline of medieval English administration, and the book survives at the National Archives today as one of the most cited documents in English history.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The Battle of Hastings (1066) was the indispensable military victory; without it there would have been no kingdom to survey.
• The network of c.500 castles by 1100 was the physical infrastructure of Norman control alongside the documentary infrastructure of Domesday.
• Lanfranc’s Church reforms transformed Norman authority over personnel and ideology in ways the survey alone did not achieve.
• Inherited Anglo-Saxon administrative machinery — shires, sheriffs, the geld assessment in hides — made Domesday possible; the achievement is shared, not purely Norman.

A strong response weighs Domesday against Hastings, castles, the Church and inherited administration, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Daily Life: Towns, Villages and Economic Change

before.content_html:
A Norman Crust on an English Loaf

The conquest changed who held land and who lived in the castle. For most people in England, however, daily life carried on. They still ploughed the same strips, paid the same kinds of dues, attended the same parish church, and ate the same food. The novelty was the Norman lord on the hill, the French quarter at the edge of town, and the royal hunting reserve at the top of the valley. Hugh Thomas calls this pattern ‘continuity beneath rupture’ — ruling-class change on top of substantial peasant continuity. The misconception students fall into is that the conquest revolutionised peasant life immediately. It did not. The slow work of change unfolded over a century.

Anglo-Saxon Village and Manorial Life

Most English peasants in 1066 lived in villages of perhaps 20 to 60 households clustered around a parish church and a lord’s hall. They worked under the open-field system: the village’s arable land was divided into long thin strips spread across two or three great fields, and each peasant household held a portion in every field so that good and poor land was shared. Crops rotated — one field in winter wheat, one in spring barley, one fallow — to keep soil fertility. Beyond the arable lay common pasture, common meadow for hay, and common woodland for fuel and pannage (acorn-feeding pigs).

Key Fact

Domesday Book records most peasants as villeins (working a substantial holding for the lord), bordars (smaller holdings, owing labour service) or cottars (cottagers with little land, working for daily wages or food). Around 10% of the population in 1086 were still slaves, mostly in the south-west, although slavery was already declining.

Roles, Seasons and Food

Peasant work followed the agricultural calendar. Spring brought ploughing and sowing; summer, weeding and haymaking; August and September, harvest and threshing; autumn, ploughing again and slaughter of livestock that could not be fed through winter; winter, threshing, repairs, weaving and salting. Most peasants ate a coarse bread of barley, rye or maslin, pottage of dried peas and beans flavoured with onions or herbs, occasional cheese and meat at festivals. Norman lords ate better — wheat bread, more meat, imported wine — but the daily routine of the manor changed only slightly.

Towns and Markets Before and After 1066

Late Anglo-Saxon England was unusually urbanised by 11th-century European standards. London, York, Winchester, Norwich, Lincoln and Thetford each had thousands of inhabitants, weekly markets, mints and craft quarters. The Normans intensified this urban growth: they granted new market charters, founded boroughs at strategic points (often beneath new castles), and established French quarters for incoming Norman merchants and settlers in major towns. At Norwich and Nottingham these French quarters had their own street plans alongside the Anglo-Saxon old town — visible in archaeology and in surviving street names today.

When the Normans took Norwich after the conquest, they laid out a new market and street grid south of the Anglo-Saxon town centre. Domesday calls it the novus burgus — the new borough — and records a population of French-speaking incomers settled there to trade. The new market eclipsed the older Tombland and is still the main market square in modern Norwich. Similar French quarters appeared at Nottingham, Northampton, Southampton and elsewhere; in each case Norman merchants, builders and clergy congregated near the castle and the new cathedral, distinct from the existing English population.

Forest Law and Royal Hunting Reserves

For peasants on the edge of forests, Norman rule meant a sharp loss of rights. Vast tracts of countryside were declared royal hunting reserves under forest law: villagers who had taken firewood, gathered fallen timber, snared rabbits or grazed pigs in the woodland for generations could now be blinded, mutilated or executed for poaching. The most notorious creation was the New Forest in Hampshire, made by clearing villages of their inhabitants — a piece of bald rural displacement on which the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle remarks bitterly. Forest law existed alongside common law, and royal foresters policed it through their own courts.

Changing Landscapes: Castles, Parks and Burhs

Norman lords reshaped the landscape in ways that ordinary villagers could see. New castles cleared rows of houses; at Lincoln, 166 English homes were demolished to make space for the new motte-and-bailey. Lordly deer parks began appearing around manor houses, separating lordly leisure from peasant work. The old Anglo-Saxon burhs (fortified towns) were modified or supplemented by Norman castles inside them, while many new market settlements grew up at castle gates. The visual impact was clear: where there had been timber halls and church towers, there were now stone keeps and motte mounds dominating the skyline.

Key Fact

Norman forest law placed huge tracts of countryside under royal hunting privilege. Peasants lost the right to take firewood, snare game or graze pigs without paying fines, and savage penalties — including blinding and mutilation — were imposed for breaches.

Continuity for Most

Despite all these changes, daily life for most peasants kept its rhythm. The same fields were ploughed, the same parish church was attended, the same crops were rotated. Old English remained the language of the village; Latin and French ran the courts and the great houses. Marriage was still arranged within local communities. The big shifts were urban (French quarters, new markets), legal (forest law, the murdrum fine, primogeniture) and architectural (castles and cathedrals), but in the cottages of Yorkshire and Wessex, the conquest did not change the calendar of work.

Anglo-Saxon law had given women relatively wide rights to hold land, make wills and seek divorce; surviving wills show women bequeathing estates in their own name. Norman customary law was less generous on inheritance, restricting widows’ rights to dower-portions of their husbands’ estates and channelling new estates through male primogeniture. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and other 11th-century sources record cases of widows of dispossessed thegns being married off to incoming Normans — a way of transferring land into Norman hands without further bloodshed. For peasant women, daily working life carried on more or less unchanged, but legally the position of higher-status English women was reduced.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark ‘Two Ways Similar or Different’ question on Anglo-Saxon and Norman daily life, choose two genuinely contrasting features and develop them. Examples: (1) Both societies organised farming through the open-field system with strips, but the Normans added forest law and lordly deer parks that restricted peasant access to woodland. (2) Both used markets and towns, but the Normans created French quarters in major towns such as Norwich and Nottingham, separating Norman incomers from the existing English population. Examiners reward clear named examples developed with detail, not generic phrases like ‘life was hard for peasants’.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of life in an Anglo-Saxon village in the years before 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Villages were typically 20 to 60 households clustered around a parish church and the lord’s hall, with houses of timber and thatch.
• Arable land was farmed in the open-field system — long thin strips spread across two or three great fields, with each peasant holding strips in each so good and poor land were shared.
• Crops rotated between winter wheat, spring barley and fallow on a two- or three-field system, alongside common pasture, hay meadow and woodland.
• Most peasants ate coarse bread of barley, rye or maslin, pottage of dried peas and beans, and occasional cheese or meat at festivals.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon and Norman daily life were similar.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Both societies organised arable farming through the open-field system, with peasants holding strips of land in two or three great fields around their village.
• Both relied on the agricultural calendar of ploughing, sowing, haymaking, harvest and slaughter, with the same crops of wheat, rye, barley and oats.
• Both used markets and towns — London, York, Winchester, Norwich, Lincoln continued as major commercial centres after 1066.
• In both periods most peasants attended their parish church for Sunday worship and for baptisms, marriages and funerals, with the parish system continuing intact.
[4 marks — 2 marks per similarity: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon and Norman daily life were different.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Two Ways Similar or Different
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Norman forest law placed vast tracts of countryside under royal hunting reserves, with savage penalties for poaching, taking firewood or grazing pigs — restrictions unknown before 1066.
• Major towns such as Norwich and Nottingham now had French quarters — new boroughs around the castle settled by Norman merchants and craftsmen, distinct from the existing English population.
• The Normans introduced lordly deer parks attached to manor houses, separating elite hunting leisure from peasant working land in a way Anglo-Saxon halls had not.
• Castles such as Lincoln were built by demolishing rows of English houses (166 at Lincoln), reshaping the urban landscape under Norman lordship.
[4 marks — 2 marks per difference: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of forest law on the lives of ordinary English people between 1066 and 1100.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Forest law placed huge tracts of countryside under royal hunting privilege, with peasants on the edges losing customary rights to gather firewood, snare rabbits, take fallen timber or graze pigs in the woodland.
• Penalties were savage by the standards of common law — blinding, mutilation, sometimes execution — and policing was carried out by separate royal foresters whose courts cut across ordinary local justice.
• At the New Forest in Hampshire, William cleared villages of their inhabitants to create the reserve — a stark act of rural displacement remembered bitterly by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.
• Forest law generated significant royal income from fines on those who breached it, intensifying the financial pressure on peasant communities adjacent to royal forests.

Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the new French quarters in major English towns after 1066.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, French quarters at Norwich, Nottingham, Northampton and Southampton gave Norman merchants, craftsmen and clergy their own boroughs alongside the Anglo-Saxon old towns — physical separation of the two communities within walking distance.
• They concentrated incoming Norman skills (stonemasonry, leatherwork, fine cloth) and money in distinct urban quarters, accelerating the growth of late 11th-century English towns.
• Domesday records the new boroughs (novus burgus) at several towns, suggesting royal interest in registering and taxing the new settlements separately from the older English ones.
• Significance over time: many of these French quarters became the dominant commercial centres of their towns — Norwich’s new market eclipsed the older Tombland and is still the main market square today.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that the Norman Conquest brought little real change to the daily life of ordinary English people.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• The open-field system, two- or three-field crop rotation and parish church framework continued largely intact — peasants ploughed the same strips and worshipped in the same churches.
• The agricultural calendar of ploughing, haymaking, harvest, threshing and slaughter was unchanged; food remained coarse bread, pottage and occasional meat for most.
• Old English remained the everyday language of the village; Latin and French ran the courts and great houses but did not penetrate the cottage.
• Domesday confirms most peasants still lived as villeins, bordars or cottars on the same manors, simply with a Norman name at the top of the entry rather than an English one.

Arguments to weigh against:
• Norman forest law restricted peasant access to woodland, game and grazing across huge tracts of countryside — a sharp legal innovation with savage penalties (blinding, mutilation, execution).
• Castles such as Lincoln were built by demolishing rows of English houses (166 at Lincoln), changing the look and feel of major towns immediately.
• French quarters at Norwich, Nottingham and elsewhere imposed new urban centres on existing towns, separating Norman from English populations and shifting commercial gravity.
• Lordly deer parks, the murdrum fine and the new dominance of stone castles and cathedrals reshaped the landscape and legal life of England by 1100.

A strong response weighs continuity in rural life against urban, legal and landscape change, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

lessons.title: Lanfranc and the Reform of the English Church

before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on Lanfranc, separate significance at the time from significance over time. At the time, his replacement of Anglo-Saxon bishops, the 1075 London council and the cathedral building programme delivered Norman political control over the English Church. Over time, his cathedrals stand to this day, his Canterbury-York settlement shaped English ecclesiastical politics for centuries, and his reform of Church courts paved the way for the long-running clash with royal authority that ran through the medieval period. Examiners reward students who hold both timescales in view.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Lanfranc’s reform of the English Church between 1070 and 1089.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He replaced almost all Anglo-Saxon bishops with Normans or Norman-trained clergy by 1080, leaving Wulfstan of Worcester as the leading English exception kept on for his reputation.
• At the 1075 council of London he tightened Church discipline — banning simony, regulating clerical marriage, reviving synods — and ordered several rural sees to move into towns (Sherborne to Salisbury, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln).
• He drove a great cathedral-building programme in the Romanesque style imported from Normandy: Canterbury, Lincoln, Old Sarum, St Albans, Worcester and Durham among others were all begun or rebuilt under his archiepiscopate.
• In 1072 at Windsor he secured a written profession from Thomas of Bayeux acknowledging Canterbury’s primacy over York, settling the long-running dispute in Canterbury’s favour.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the deposition of Stigand in 1070 for Norman control of England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, Stigand’s removal at the Easter council at Winchester in 1070 cleared the way for Lanfranc’s appointment, which gave William a loyal reformer in the senior English see.
• It also justified retrospectively William’s 1066 invasion: Stigand’s pluralism (holding Canterbury and Winchester at once) and uncanonical pallium from antipope Benedict X had been used by Pope Alexander II to bless the Norman invasion.
• It opened the door to a wider purge: by 1080 almost all English bishops had been replaced with Normans, transforming the institutional voice of the English Church.
• Significance over time: Stigand’s deposition marked the start of a programme of Norman ecclesiastical control that survived through Lanfranc’s death in 1089 and shaped Church appointments for the rest of William’s and his sons’ reigns.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the cathedral building programme in Norman England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Cathedrals were rebuilt at unprecedented scale — Canterbury (begun 1070), Lincoln (1072), St Albans (1077), Old Sarum (1075), Durham (1093) — far larger than the Anglo-Saxon churches they replaced.
• They used the round-arched Romanesque style imported from Normandy, with thick walls, massive piers and small windows giving the buildings a heavy, fortress-like feel.
• Several cathedrals were relocated from rural sites into nearby towns at the 1075 council of London — Sherborne to Old Sarum, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln — tying ecclesiastical centres to Norman urban and military networks.
• The buildings doubled as visible symbols of Norman authority — like castles, but for the spiritual rather than the military hierarchy.
[4 marks — 2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development.]

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the 1075 council of London for the Norman reform of the English Church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• At the time, the council revived the practice of regular synods and established a forum for ongoing reform of Church discipline; it banned simony, regulated clerical marriage and tightened canon law.
• It moved several rural Anglo-Saxon sees into towns (Sherborne to Salisbury, Selsey to Chichester, Dorchester to Lincoln) — aligning ecclesiastical centres with Norman urban networks of castles, courts and markets.
• It strengthened the office of archdeacon and clarified the separation of Church courts from secular courts, deepening the Church’s institutional autonomy.
• Significance over time: the disciplinary measures of 1075 became the template for English ecclesiastical councils through the 12th century, and the urban relocations are still visible in the modern map of English cathedral cities.

Mastering: Significance shown both at the time and over time, with precise examples.
Secure: Clear significance explained with relevant detail.
Developing: Some significance with limited examples.
Emerging: Simple description; significance unclear.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Lanfranc’s appointment on the leadership of the English Church.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Within a decade almost every English diocese had a Norman or Norman-trained bishop — Lanfranc himself at Canterbury, Thomas of Bayeux at York, Walkelin at Winchester, Remigius at Lincoln — transforming the personnel of the English Church.
• The exceptions are striking: Wulfstan of Worcester was kept on for his reputation, becoming the only Anglo-Saxon bishop still in office at William’s death in 1087 — a deliberate gesture of continuity in an otherwise wholesale replacement.
• Lanfranc and the new Norman bishops drove the cathedral building programme, the 1075 council of London and the Canterbury-vs-York primacy dispute — the institutional Church now spoke with a Norman voice on every major issue.
• Lanfranc also acted as William’s effective regent during the Earls’ Revolt of 1075 while the king was in Normandy — showing how thoroughly the new ecclesiastical leadership was tied into royal politics.

Mastering: Multiple effects developed with named individuals and clear causal chains.
Secure: Two or more effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified with limited explanation.
Emerging: Simple points; little development.

practice_questions.text: Argue, using examples from across the period 1066 to 1100, that Lanfranc’s reform of the Church was as important as the Norman land settlement in establishing Norman rule in England.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include arguments in support:
• By 1080 almost every English diocese had a Norman bishop, transforming the institutional voice of the English Church alongside the transformation of the lay landholding class.
• The cathedral building programme — Canterbury, Lincoln, Old Sarum, St Albans, Durham, Worcester — visibly stamped Norman authority on the English landscape, just as castles did.
• The 1075 council of London tightened Church discipline and reorganised dioceses to align with Norman urban centres, paralleling the way the land settlement aligned political power with new tenants-in-chief.
• Lanfranc acted as effective regent during the 1075 Earls’ Revolt, showing that the Church reform underpinned royal authority at moments of crisis as well as in routine government.

Arguments to weigh against:
• The redistribution of land to around 180 tenants-in-chief recorded in Domesday transformed the social structure of England in ways no Church reform alone could match.
• The network of c.500 castles by 1100 was the physical infrastructure of military control — without castles, neither the lay nor the ecclesiastical settlement could have been enforced.
• The Harrying of the North and the wider crushing of revolt 1067–71 broke organised Anglo-Saxon resistance before either reform programme could take effect.
• Inherited Anglo-Saxon government — shires, sheriffs, the geld — provided the day-to-day administrative machinery that the Norman elite, lay and ecclesiastical, used.

A strong response weighs Church reform against land settlement, castles, military victory and inherited administration, reaching a substantiated overall judgement.

Mastering: Sustained argument across the period with embedded evidence and a justified judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with relevant evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some argument; evidence may be limited.
Emerging: Simple points; little argument or judgement.

lessons.title: Monasticism, Learning and the Investiture Controversy

before.content_html:
Monasticism, Learning and a Brewing Crisis

The Norman reform of the English Church did not stop with bishops and cathedrals. Norman lords also founded new monasteries, drove a programme of monastic learning, and reorganised the Latin schools that trained the next generation of clergy. By the end of William I’s reign, monasticism was a Norman as much as an English institution. But the closer the Norman Church grew to the papacy, the more the issue of investiture — who had the right to appoint bishops and abbots — threatened to break the partnership of king and Church. By the 1090s, England was drawn into the European-wide controversy that began with Pope Gregory VII.

A New Wave of Norman Abbeys

After 1066, Norman lords founded or refounded a remarkable number of monasteries. The most famous is Battle Abbey in Sussex, founded by William as penance for the bloodshed of Hastings; the abbey’s high altar was placed on the spot where Harold was said to have fallen. Other major Norman abbeys included Selby (1069), Tewkesbury (rebuilt from the 1070s), Shrewsbury (1083) and Bermondsey. By 1100 there were perhaps 250 monasteries in England, up from around 60 in 1066. The new houses were typically Benedictine, often staffed in the early years by monks brought from Norman houses such as Caen, Bec or Jumièges.

Key Fact

The number of monasteries in England rose from around 60 in 1066 to roughly 250 by 1100. Battle Abbey in Sussex was founded by William I as penance for the deaths at Hastings, with its high altar marking the place Harold was said to have fallen.

Monastic Life

Most Norman abbeys followed the Rule of St Benedict, the framework that governed monastic life across western Europe. Monks lived a tightly regulated day — the eight services of the Divine Office from Matins through to Compline, periods of manual work, periods of reading and study, and the sleeping and eating that fitted between them. Hospitality, charity to the poor, and prayers for the souls of dead patrons were all standard duties. Wealthy patrons (kings, tenants-in-chief and bishops) gave land in exchange for these prayers, which is how monasteries became economically powerful.

Cluniac Influence

Some Norman foundations followed the more demanding Cluniac reform: a network of monasteries linked to the great abbey of Cluny in Burgundy, founded in 910. Cluniac houses placed unusual emphasis on the elaborate liturgy of prayer (singing the Divine Office at length), held themselves independent of local lords, and looked to the Pope rather than to bishops or kings as their ultimate authority. The English Cluniac priory at Lewes was founded in 1078 by William de Warenne and his wife Gundrada. The arrival of Cluniac houses tied the Norman English Church into a wider European reform movement that pushed back against royal control of religious life.

Founding an abbey was a Norman lord’s way of doing several jobs at once. Religiously, monks would pray for his soul and the souls of his family in perpetuity. Politically, an abbey on his lands was a stable centre that strengthened his hold on the area. Economically, the abbey would clear forest, drain wetland and improve the value of donated estates. Culturally, it was a sign of status — a Norman lord with an abbey to his name was visibly part of the European Christian elite. The result was the wave of new foundations from Battle (1067) through Selby (1069), Shrewsbury (1083) and beyond.

Schools, Latin and the Vernacular

Norman monasteries and cathedrals were the schools of England. Cathedral schools at Canterbury, Lincoln and Durham trained boys in Latin grammar, rhetoric, music and basic arithmetic; the more advanced schools also taught the seven liberal arts. Lanfranc himself had taught at Bec, where he ran a school of European reputation. The Latin language was the lingua franca of educated Europe, used in royal writs, Church liturgy and Domesday Book itself.

Below the elite, however, the language story was layered. Norman lords and clerks spoke Anglo-Norman at home and in court; English peasants spoke Old English in the village; Latin ran the Church and chancery. The result was a trilingual ruling culture in which English persisted as the everyday speech of the majority, gradually picking up French vocabulary that would reshape it into Middle English by the 12th and 13th centuries. The vernacular Anglo-Saxon Chronicle was still being written in some monasteries (notably Peterborough) into the 12th century.

Key Fact

Norman England was a trilingual society. Norman lords and clerks spoke Anglo-Norman; English peasants spoke Old English; Latin ran the Church, the schools and royal documents like Domesday. By 1100 the three languages were starting to fuse, beginning the long change toward Middle English.

William I and the Papacy

William’s reform partnership with Lanfranc had to be balanced against the demands of Pope Gregory VII, the most assertive reform pope of the 11th century. Gregory pushed to end lay investiture — the appointment of bishops by kings and emperors — and to subordinate temporal rulers to papal authority. In 1080 Gregory pressed William to do homage to him for England, as some other rulers had done. William refused. He paid the customary annual tribute (Peter’s Pence), but he kept the right to appoint English bishops and to control papal access to England. Lanfranc supported William’s line, framing it as protection of the English Church against meddling from outside.

William II and Anselm: the English Investiture Controversy

After Lanfranc died in 1089, William II (Rufus) deliberately left the see of Canterbury vacant for four years, pocketing its revenues. Pressed by serious illness and his bishops, he finally appointed Anselm — Lanfranc’s pupil at Bec, by then the abbey’s abbot — in 1093. Anselm proved less compliant than Lanfranc. He insisted on recognising Pope Urban II in defiance of William’s preferred candidate; he refused to pay William large sums in gratitude for his appointment; he asserted that the Church owed obedience to the Pope on disputed matters of investiture. The clash with Rufus broke into the open after 1095. Anselm went into exile rather than accept what he saw as royal interference, and the dispute continued under Henry I until a compromise was reached in 1107.

William Rufus needed money. Crushing the 1088 rebellion, defending Normandy against his brother Robert Curthose, and paying mercenaries all required cash. The Church was wealthy: tenants-in-chief like the bishop of Durham held vast estates, and vacant sees produced revenue every month they remained empty. Rufus exploited the situation by leaving Canterbury vacant for four years (1089–93), holding the revenues for himself, and trying to install bishops on his own terms. Anselm’s clash with him was therefore part of a wider royal pattern of squeezing Church wealth that horrified contemporaries and fed twelfth-century stories of Rufus as an impious king. Some monastic chroniclers even wrote of his death in the New Forest in 1100 as God’s judgement.

Key Fact

Where Lanfranc had partnered loyally with William I against the papacy, Anselm clashed with William II from 1093 over Church appointments and obedience to Rome. Anselm’s exile drew England into the Investiture Controversy that ran across European politics from Pope Gregory VII’s reforms onwards.
before.exam_tip_html: For an ‘Explain Significance’ question on Anselm and the Investiture Controversy, separate timing and consequence. At the time, the dispute deprived William II of Canterbury revenues and forced Anselm into exile. Over time, it set the pattern of Church-state conflict that ran through the 12th century and dragged England into a European-wide reform argument it had stayed clear of under William I and Lanfranc. Examiners reward students who can name Pope Gregory VII, Pope Urban II and Anselm precisely and link the English row to the wider European one.

practice_questions.marks:

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Norman monastic foundations such as Battle Abbey for the consolidation of Norman rule.
